blocks.title: A function is a mapping with obligations
paragraphs: A function must assign every domain object exactly one output in the codomain. Injectivity and surjectivity ask different questions about that valid mapping. A relation is more general and is checked against its own quantified property definitions.

blocks.title: Check function status before extra properties
paragraphs: For f:A→B, verify three requirements: every input in A has an output, every input has only one output, and every output lies in B. An omitted input, conflicting outputs, or an output outside B prevents the table from defining that function.
The codomain is declared; the image is the set of outputs actually reached. They need not be equal. A formula also needs these checks for every allowed input, not only a few convenient values.

blocks.title: Keep domain, codomain and image separate
paragraphs: Let A={a,b,c}, B={1,2,3,4}, and define f(a)=2, f(b)=1, f(c)=3. This is a function: each domain object has one permitted output. Its image is {1,2,3}.

It is injective because the three inputs have distinct outputs. It is not surjective onto B because 4 has no preimage, so it is not bijective. If the declared codomain is instead {1,2,3}, the same assignments form a bijection.

Injective means f(x)=f(y) implies x=y for all domain x,y. Surjective means every codomain b has some domain x with f(x)=b. Bijective means both; many-to-one and a missing codomain value are different failure modes.

blocks.title: Build the constraints into a candidate mapping
paragraphs: Start by listing the required domain, codomain and properties. For an injection reserve distinct outputs for distinct inputs; for a surjection ensure every codomain value is reached. Then check totality and unique outputs as well as the requested property.
For finite sets, more domain elements than codomain elements prevents injectivity, and fewer domain elements prevents surjectivity. These are useful impossibility checks before constructing a table.

To construct a surjective but noninjective function from {a,b,c} to {0,1}, one choice is a↦0, b↦1, c↦1. Both outputs occur, and b,c collide. The alternative a↦1, b↦0, c↦0 also works; exact agreement with a sample table is not required.

blocks.title: Translate relation properties into all-pair obligations
paragraphs: A relation R on A is a subset of A×A. Reflexive means every x∈A has (x,x)∈R. Symmetric means (x,y)∈R implies (y,x)∈R. Transitive means (x,y)∈R and (y,z)∈R imply (x,z)∈R for every triple.

A relation is an equivalence relation when all three properties hold. To disprove a property, give a missing diagonal pair, an asymmetric pair, or a composable pair of edges with a missing shortcut, respectively. A property may hold vacuously when there is no antecedent configuration.

blocks.title: Check all requirements of equivalence
paragraphs: On A={0,1,2}, let xRy mean x and y have the same parity. The explicit relation is {(0,0),(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(2,2)}. Every diagonal is present; reversing any listed pair stays in the relation; composing same-parity pairs keeps the endpoints the same parity. It is an equivalence relation.

Its equivalence classes are {0,2} and {1}: the classes group objects related to one another. For a nontransitive contrast, on {0,1,2} take R={(0,1),(1,2)}. The pairs (0,1),(1,2) are present but (0,2) is missing, so transitivity fails.

The empty relation on a nonempty set is symmetric and transitive, because there are no pairs satisfying their antecedents, but it is not reflexive. Domain information is essential when classifying a relation.

blocks.title: One example rarely settles an infinite claim
paragraphs: For an arbitrary-domain injection proof, begin with arbitrary x,y and f(x)=f(y), then derive x=y. For surjectivity, begin with an arbitrary codomain value and construct a valid preimage. Finite enumeration checks a finite table only.

Do not swap the roles of domain and codomain or mistake a function’s image for its declared codomain. Before calling a relation transitive, check every composable pair, including cases with repeated vertices.

blocks.title: Check definitions with the correct quantifiers
paragraphs: First establish a valid function, then test distinct-input outputs and coverage of the codomain separately. For relations, check each property’s universal obligation or supply a specific counterexample. Constructions require constraints, not one preferred representation.

cards.prompt: Which three conditions establish f:A→B is a function?
cards.answer: Every input in A has an output, each has exactly one output, and every output is in B. Extra mapping properties are checked only after these conditions hold.

cards.prompt: How does the image differ from the codomain?
cards.answer: The codomain is the declared target set; the image consists of outputs actually attained. Surjectivity means they are equal.

cards.prompt: How should a learner-created function be checked?
cards.answer: Check its entire stated domain and codomain, totality, unique outputs and every requested property. Any mapping satisfying these requirements is valid, even if it differs from a reference table.

cards.prompt: What is an injectivity proof’s usual logical starting point?
cards.answer: Let x,y be arbitrary domain elements and assume f(x)=f(y); derive x=y. To refute it, give distinct inputs with equal outputs.

cards.prompt: What does a surjectivity proof need for an arbitrary target b?
cards.answer: An input x in the declared domain satisfying f(x)=b. The target b is arbitrary in the codomain, so every target is covered.

cards.prompt: Which properties define an equivalence relation?
cards.answer: Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Each must hold on the declared set; satisfying only two does not suffice.

cards.prompt: What is a witness that transitivity fails?
cards.answer: Objects x,y,z with xRy and yRz but not xRz. All objects and relation facts must belong to the same declared structure.

cards.prompt: Is the empty relation on a nonempty set an equivalence relation?
cards.answer: No. It is symmetric and transitive vacuously, but lacks every required diagonal pair, so it is not reflexive.

guided.title: Construct two different valid mappings
guided.prompt: Construct two distinct functions from {a,b,c} to {0,1}, each surjective and noninjective. Explain all required properties.
rubric: Each input has exactly one output in {0,1}.
Both target values are attained in each function.
At least two distinct inputs share an output in each function.
reference: One function sends a↦0,b↦1,c↦1. Another sends a↦1,b↦0,c↦0.
Both are total, hit both outputs, and map b,c to the same output. These are examples, not the only accepted functions.

guided.title: Justify an equivalence relation
guided.prompt: On {0,1,2}, define xRy when x and y have the same parity. Justify reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, and identify its classes.
rubric: Every object has its own parity.
Reversing an equal-parity pair preserves the condition.
Two same-parity links force the endpoints to have the same parity.
Classes cover the domain without overlap and contain exactly the mutually related objects.
reference: The relation is {(0,0),(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(2,2)}. Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity follow from equality of parity.
The classes are {0,2} and {1}. A list of pairs alone should be accompanied by the required reasoning.
